dek: The best AI model for agentic tool use is only part of the system. Production reliability comes from containing handoff, waiting, authority, and verification failures around it.
rel: Gemini 3.8 Flash: fast coding, uneven judgment beyond the patch
MiniMax M3 review: strong coding, uneven reliability
GPT-6 Astra in Production: The Agent Is Better, the System Still Decides
body: A background agent finished its work, but the planner kept scheduling wakeups and polling files. The turn never ended, so the notification path could not take over. That is the failure this architecture must contain. A model can issue plausible tools and still misunderstand the harness that makes those tools useful.

The turn controller owns continuation, waiting, and termination. It should distinguish useful parallel work from waiting on work already launched. A GitHub issue captures the trap: «none of the ~8+ scheduled wakeups in this session ever actually fired». We agree with its diagnosis: control flow, not missing model intelligence, made those calls dead weight.
none of the ~8+ scheduled wakeups in this session ever actually fired

Make waiting a state transition, not a prose intention. The controller should yield until notification or another useful task becomes ready. The GitHub report says background agents already deliver an automatic «task-notification»; the architecture should trust that event and prohibit polling loops unless the workflow explicitly requires them. Stop the loop.

This boundary contains repeated no-op calls and wasted tokens. It does not guarantee that a model will obey a stop instruction. Treat the harness as the authority: it records task state, accepts completion events, and closes the turn when the next action would only recheck unchanged state. That is the boundary.

body.label: Controller state-transition sketch
body.source:
if background_task_running:
    state = WAITING
    end_turn()

on_completion_notification(task_id):
    state = VERIFYING
    verify(task_id)

body: The tool gateway defines what the model can touch. It validates arguments, checks permissions, and returns structured outcomes; it does not treat a generated call as an authorized action. This boundary matters most when an agent can edit files, execute commands, or operate a browser. A successful tool call proves execution, not correctness or safety. Keep the boundary firm.

body.alt: A gateway checks tool requests before they reach a locked workshop.
body.caption: The gateway controls permissions and validates every proposed action.

body: A dev.to engineer retraced Claude Code against several Anthropic-compatible endpoints using a real file-writing task. The engineer reported «worked first try» for DeepSeek, Qwen, and GLM, and a Kimi run that needed a retry. We agree that compatibility can make a model swap mechanically simple. We do not read a tiny file task as evidence of equivalent long-horizon behavior.

The same write-up warns that a secondary background model setting can quietly point at an endpoint the gateway does not serve. That is a configuration boundary, not a reasoning defect. Validate every model role at startup, then fail loudly when a route is missing. Silent failure makes a healthy primary model look unreliable.

Keep schemas and permissions outside model choice. The gateway should reject malformed arguments, enforce least privilege, and attach a stable task identifier to each operation. If a model repeats a call, the gateway can detect duplication or require explicit approval. The model proposes; the gateway decides what actually runs.

One model should not own every job in an agent loop. The planner turns a goal into bounded work; workers perform edits or exploration; a verifier checks the result. The separation limits drift because no worker can silently redefine the acceptance criteria and declare itself done.

body.alt: Planner, worker, and verifier operate in separate work areas.
body.caption: Separate roles keep execution from quietly redefining success.

body: An X post describes a Claude Code arrangement with Opus planning, Sonnet workers, and Fable evaluating completion. The poster reports that routine work goes to the workers and the evaluator inspects the transcript at turn boundaries. We include it as a reported pattern, not a benchmark. Its useful idea is role separation, with explicit authority limits.

A dev.to discussion presents GPT-6 Sol as a sustained-work option and Luna as a volume route, but also relays a developer complaint that Sol «wasted 80% getting side tracked» as an orchestrator. We agree with the warning against assigning one model every role. We are not convinced the anecdote proves Luna is the right replacement; the evidence points to splitting orchestration from routine work, then testing both routes.

Choose a worker by the work it must complete, not by a broad capability label. A coding worker needs repository access and executable checks. An explorer needs read access and a concise handoff. A planner needs enough context to preserve the task contract. The controller owns role assignment and can stop any worker that exceeds its boundary.

body.caption: Role boundaries keep planning, execution, checking, and authority distinct.
An X post describes a planner-worker-evaluator arrangement with routine subagents and transcript checks, illustrating role separation.

body: A weak task contract turns tool use into guesswork. The contract should name the desired outcome, permitted tools, forbidden changes, and evidence required for completion. It must also state what happens when evidence is missing. The model can reason over the contract; the harness should enforce its hard edges.

A GitHub report describes Sonnet repeatedly calling a wakeup tool as it waited for delegated work. Its author summarized the behavior as «I should keep taking small actions to check in». That is a useful failure description, not a claim about every Sonnet session. The issue also says guidance reduced the spiral, which shows that prompt and harness changes can alter behavior.
I should keep taking small actions to check in

We agree with the engineer who separated a scheduled wakeup from ending the turn. The mechanism only helps if the controller lets the turn end. Put that condition in executable policy: after scheduling a wait, disallow further tools in that turn. Better still, use a completion notification where the runtime provides one, then reserve timers for self-paced workflows.

Contracts also protect against confident scope drift. A coding agent may satisfy tests yet violate an instruction or change unrelated files. The planner should turn acceptance criteria into checkable predicates, and the verifier should inspect both outputs and constraints. If the criteria are ambiguous, the system should ask a human rather than broaden its authority.

A tool result is evidence, not a verdict. The verification gate compares the artifact with the task contract, runs relevant checks, and decides whether to accept, retry, or escalate. For code, that can include tests, lint, and diff review. For other tools, it means checking the resulting state through an independent read.

The X poster assigns a separate verifier role to tests and linters; the GitHub issue shows how polling can masquerade as progress. Together they support an important boundary: verification should consume observable artifacts, not the model's claim that it has checked them. We agree with that architecture, but the reports do not establish its measured reliability.

A separate evaluator can inspect a transcript and identify drift, but it must not replace deterministic checks. A model judging another model can share blind spots or misread the same tool output. Use model review for semantic criteria that lack a direct test; use the harness for facts that can be executed or queried.

This gate contains false completion and unnecessary retries. Record the evidence behind every decision: tool outputs, changed files, check results, and unresolved criteria. When evidence conflicts, stop the agent and route the case to a human. Do not let a fluent summary erase a failing check.

Astra can perform powerful computer-based work, but capability raises the cost of weak controls. A dev.to essay reports that GPT-6 Astra crossed a cybersecurity threshold and describes safeguards and restricted access around sensitive capabilities. We should not turn those claims into a generic model ranking. They support a narrower design rule: tool authority belongs to policy and deployment controls, not model judgment.

body.alt: A powerful machine works behind a controlled safety enclosure.
body.caption: Authority and blast radius belong to external controls.

body: CoT monitoring is no longer enough on its own

Keep credentials, network access, filesystem scope, and irreversible actions behind the gateway. Require approval for actions with material external consequences. A model that can plan a sequence should not automatically receive permission to execute every step. The planner proposes; policy grants a limited capability for a specific task.

We agree with the Astra essay's emphasis on the monitoring problem, especially its warning that «CoT monitoring is no longer enough on its own». A production system needs observable action logs and outcome checks. We disagree with any architecture that treats a model's internal explanation as a safety boundary; external controls can deny a dangerous tool call regardless of how persuasive the explanation sounds.

The failure contained here is unauthorized impact, not bad reasoning. Sandboxing limits what a confused worker can change. Approval gates preserve human control over high-impact actions. Audit records make investigation possible after a failure. None of these controls makes the model harmless, so keep the blast radius small.

The router should price accepted work, not just tokens. Retries, long context, verification, and human review all affect the bill. Registry rates give GPT-6 Sol and Claude Sonnet 5.5 the same listed input and output prices, but that does not make their end-to-end agent costs equal. Measure completion quality and total work on your own tasks.

A dev.to write-up on Sol and Luna argues for routing ambient classification away from a frontier model. Its useful principle is specialization, not its unsupported universal conclusions. The posted model descriptions frame Sol for sustained agentic work and Luna for ambient tasks; treat those as starting hypotheses, then compare accepted outcomes and failure costs.

We retraced one engineer's file-writing experiment, which reported «worked first try» for several models and a retry for Kimi. The test is too small to settle repository work, multi-step tool use, or reliable completion. We agree with its practical lesson: adapter compatibility gets you to a trial, not through production qualification.

Set escalation rules before launch. Route routine, low-risk work to a cheaper worker only when the verifier can cheaply detect errors. Send ambiguous planning or high-impact decisions to a stronger route or a human. The best LLM for agentic tool use is the one that meets your task contract at acceptable total cost under your own harness.

No architecture prevents every model from misreading a goal, every tool from returning misleading state, or every evaluation from missing a rare failure. The final boundary is operational: monitor accepted work, rejected work, retries, stalled turns, permission denials, and human overrides. Those signals reveal where the pattern is failing.

Model reports split across task types. One dev.to file-writing test showed several compatible models completing a small task; a GitHub issue recorded persistent polling behavior in a specific Sonnet workflow, with a similar complaint about Opus. We do not infer a universal winner from either side. The evidence favors a governed architecture because failures cross model and harness boundaries.

A useful production pattern makes failure legible. Preserve task contracts, tool traces, verification results, and route decisions. Replay representative failures after model, prompt, adapter, or runtime changes. If a model update changes turn endings or tool selection, the rollout should pause before that behavior reaches high-impact work.

The pattern still cannot contain an unknown failure that passes every check and causes harm outside the observed boundary. Keep consequential actions reversible where possible, limit exposure, and retain a human stop path. That is the remaining engineering work: not confidence in a model, but a system that can detect and absorb its mistakes.

body: What is the best AI model for agentic tool use?

There is no universal best AI model for agentic tool use; choose by task, harness, and verified outcome. A dev.to file-writing test found several compatible models could complete a small task, but that does not establish long-running reliability. Compare candidate models on your tool schemas, turn control, acceptance checks, and total cost per accepted task.
How do I stop an AI agent from endlessly calling tools?

Make waiting and termination explicit states in the controller. A GitHub issue describes repeated wakeup calls that never fired because the agent continued the turn instead of yielding. After a genuine wait is scheduled, end the turn; prefer completion notifications for background work, and block redundant polling unless a task contract requires it.
How should I compare AI models for agentic tool use?

Compare models on the same task contract, tool permissions, runtime, and verification gate. Record successful completion, tool errors, retries, drift, and human review rather than relying on a single file-writing result or model claim. Include adapter and background-role configuration, since a compatible primary endpoint can still fail if another configured role is unavailable.
